Payroll tax audits, state assessments and amended returns for employers
An IRS employment tax audit is an examination of an employer’s payroll tax returns, and it can end with no change, a refund or additional tax. Employers correct a Form 941 with Form 941-X, a Form 940 with a new Form 940 marked as amended, and a Form W-2 with Form W-2c. Form 941-X has set time limits, and state agencies run separate assessments and appeals with deadlines that vary by state and notice.
What happens in an IRS payroll tax audit?
An IRS payroll tax audit, which the IRS also calls an examination, reviews an employer’s employment tax returns by mail or in person. The IRS notifies an employer by mail, and its audits page says it will not initiate an audit by telephone. In a mail examination, a letter asks about certain return items, and IRS Publication 5146 says to send copies rather than originals, put the business name, employer identification number (EIN) and tax periods on each page, and respond by the deadline in the letter. Early on, the examiner verifies that the employer filed required information returns, such as Forms W-2 and 1099-NEC, and furnished statements to recipients. The result is either a letter saying no changes were proposed or an explanation of proposed changes.
How does the IRS decide to examine an employer’s payroll tax returns?
Selection for an IRS employment tax examination can begin with computer programs that flag returns that may be incorrect, or with compliance-project information from sources such as public and internal records. IRS Publication 5146 says the flags can be based on information returns, past examinations or issue-based projects. Being selected, the IRS says, “does not mean that you have made an error.”
What records should I expect to produce in an employment tax audit?
The IRS employment tax recordkeeping page says employment tax records should be available for IRS review and lists, among other items, the employer identification number, the amounts and dates of wage payments, employee names, Social Security numbers and dates of employment, copies of Forms W-4, the dates and amounts of tax deposits, copies of returns filed, fringe benefit records and documentation for credits claimed. The IRS says to keep all records of employment taxes for at least four years after filing the fourth-quarter return for the year. The IRS examiner manual, which is internal guidance to examiners, describes Form 4564, Information Document Request, as the enclosure that details the documents an examiner requests (IRM 4.23.3).
Can someone else represent my business in an IRS payroll tax audit?
In an examination, an employer may act for itself or use a representative who is an attorney, accountant, enrolled agent or the paid preparer who signed the return, with written authorization on Form 2848 (IRS Publication 5146). Form 2848 lets an eligible representative speak and act for the business before the IRS, Form 8821 lets a designee only see and receive the business’s tax information, and the third-party designee on Form 941 can only discuss that return’s processing questions.
How far back can an employment tax audit go, and does correcting a return change that?
The IRS says filing an amended Form 940 or an X form such as Form 941-X does not affect the period of limitation for assessment, which is generally 3 years from the date the return is filed (IRS Publication 5146). The IRS may ask an employer to extend the period on Form SS-10, and the employer may agree, agree to a limited extension or refuse. For audits in general, the IRS says it can include returns filed within the last three years, may add years if it finds a substantial error, and generally does not go back more than six years (IRS audits page).
What can I do if I disagree with the audit results?
An employer that disagrees with proposed audit changes can ask the examiner to reconsider with more information, ask for a meeting or call with the examiner’s manager, and, if there is still no agreement, request an Appeals conference by following the 30-day letter that comes with the examiner’s report (IRS Publication 5146). To go to court, an employer may file a refund suit in a U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims after paying at least the tax for one worker for one tax period and filing the matching X-form claim for refund. If the claim is disallowed or the IRS does not respond within 6 months, the employer may sue, generally no later than 2 years after the IRS informs it that the claim is disallowed.
How does the IRS examine worker classification?
In a worker classification examination, the IRS decides whether workers an employer treated as independent contractors are employees under the common law test, which weighs behavioral control, financial control and the relationship of the parties. Behavioral control is the right to direct what work is done and how, financial control includes unreimbursed expenses, investment in tools and the opportunity for profit or loss, and the relationship covers written contracts, employee-type benefits and permanency. The IRS says no one factor stands alone and each should be documented (IRS independent contractor page, Topic 762).


If a worker reclassification or Section 530 issue is not resolved and the IRS determines the employer owes tax, the employer receives Letter 3523, Notice of Employment Tax Determination Under IRC Section 7436. To seek U.S. Tax Court review, the employer must file a petition before the 91st day after the notice was mailed by certified or registered mail, or the 151st day if the notice is addressed outside the United States. The time cannot be extended, and the employer need not pay first. An employer that does not qualify for Section 530 relief may be eligible for the optional Classification Settlement Program, which, under a closing agreement, reclassifies workers for the future in an examination in exchange for reduced liability for the past treatment (IRS Publication 5146).
What is Section 530 relief?
Section 530 relief can mean an employer owes no employment tax for workers it treated as nonemployees, if it meets all three requirements in IRS Publication 1976.


1. Reporting consistency means the employer filed all required returns, including information returns such as Form 1099-NEC, consistent with treating the worker as a nonemployee, before the examination began.
2. Substantive consistency means the employer, and any predecessor, treated the worker and any similar worker as a nonemployee and not as an employee for periods after 1977 (IRS Publication 15).
3. Reasonable basis means the employer reasonably relied on a court case about federal taxes, an IRS ruling issued to it, a prior IRS audit (after 1996, one that included an employment tax examination of worker status) that did not reclassify similar workers, a significant segment of its industry’s treatment of similar workers, or other reasonable grounds such as advice from a business lawyer or accountant who knew the facts.


Section 530 applies only to worker status, not to how wages are characterized, and it does not itself determine a worker’s status. IRS guidance to examiners says an examiner must consider Section 530 first.
What is the penalty for treating employees as 1099 contractors instead of W-2 employees?
An employer that treats an employee as a contractor without a reasonable basis may be held liable for employment taxes for that worker, and in an examination the IRS may also determine penalties and interest (IRS independent contractor page, IRS Publication 5146). When an employer treated an employee as a nonemployee and has no relief, the IRS lets it figure its liability at the reduced section 3509 rates, which are not available for intentional disregard or when income tax was withheld but not Social Security or Medicare tax, and the employer cannot recover that tax from the employee. The rates below are as of October 2026 and depend on whether the employer filed the required information returns (IRS Publication 15, 26 U.S.C. 3509).

The 7.44 percent Social Security rate applies only to wages up to the Social Security wage base (VCSP frequently asked questions), and the table excludes FUTA, state taxes, information return penalties and interest.
What is the voluntary classification settlement program?
The IRS Voluntary Classification Settlement Program (VCSP) lets an eligible employer that is not under employment tax examination reclassify workers as employees for future periods by paying 10 percent of the employment tax liability that would have been due on the most recent year’s compensation at the reduced section 3509(a) rates, with no interest or penalties on that payment. The IRS says the employer will not be subject to an employment tax audit on the classification of those workers for prior years. As of October 2026, the requirements include that the employer be presently and consistently treating the workers as independent contractors or other nonemployees, have filed all required Forms 1099 for them for the 3 preceding calendar years (or the period the workers worked for it), have no current dispute with the IRS over their status, not be under employment tax examination by the IRS or under examination on the classification by the Department of Labor or a state agency, and, if the IRS or the Department of Labor previously examined the classification of those workers, have complied with the results and not be contesting the classification in court. The employer applies on Form 8952 at least 120 days before the date it wants to begin treating the workers as employees, sends no payment with the application, signs it personally rather than through a representative, and pays in full when it returns the signed closing agreement (IRS VCSP page, VCSP frequently asked questions, Instructions for Form 8952).


Hypothetical example. An employer paid one worker $50,000 in the most recent year, below the Social Security wage base, and filed the required Forms 1099. The section 3509(a) liability is 10.68 percent × $50,000 = $5,340, and the VCSP payment is 10 percent × $5,340 = $534.
How do I amend a Form 941?
Employers amend a Form 941 by filing Form 941-X, one form for each quarter corrected. The Instructions for Form 941-X say underreported and overreported amounts for the same quarter go on one form, unless the employer requests a refund, in which case it files one form for underreported amounts only and a second for overreported amounts. On Form 941-X you use the adjustment process to pay what you underreported or to apply an overreported amount as a credit on a later Form 941, you use the claim process to ask for a refund, and in the last 90 days before the time limit ends you must use the claim process. The employer checks line 1 for the adjustment process or line 2 for the claim process and explains each correction in detail on line 43. Form 941-X does not apply if the employer did not file a Form 941 for the quarter, in which case it files the Form 941.
How long do I have to correct a Form 941?
If you underreported tax on a Form 941, file Form 941-X by the due date of the return for the quarter in which you discovered the error and pay what you owe by the time you file, which the IRS says generally keeps the correction interest-free and free of failure-to-pay and failure-to-deposit penalties. The Instructions for Form 941-X add that no correction is eligible for interest-free treatment if the employer knowingly underreported, received a notice and demand for payment, received a notice of determination under section 7436, or the amounts relate to an issue raised in an examination of a prior period. For underreported tax, the due dates below are as of October 2026, and a due date that falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday moves to the next business day.


Quarter in which the error was discovered
Form 941-X due date
January to March
April 30
April to June
July 31
July to September
October 31
October to December
January 31


Hypothetical example. An error discovered in November 2026 is due January 31, 2027, a Sunday, so the due date moves to Monday, February 1, 2027.


You may correct overreported tax on a Form 941 within 3 years of the date it was filed or 2 years from the date you paid the tax, whichever is later, and a Form 941 filed before April 15 of the following year counts as filed on April 15. The Instructions for Form 941-X also say the period of limitations for correcting underreported tax is generally 3 years from the date the Form 941 was filed.
How do I correct a Form 940?
There is no X form for Form 940, the annual federal unemployment (FUTA) tax return, so an employer corrects it by filing a new Form 940 for the year being amended with the amended return box (box a) checked. The Instructions for Form 940 say to fill in all the amounts that should have been on the original, sign the form and attach an explanation. The IRS says interest-free adjustments are not available for underpaid FUTA taxes (IRS Correcting employment taxes).
How do I correct a Form W-2 I already filed?
An employer corrects a Form W-2 already filed with the Social Security Administration (SSA) by filing Form W-2c with a Form W-3c and giving the employee a corrected copy, and the 2026 General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 say to do both as soon as possible after discovering the error. The Form W-2c must be e-filed if the original Form W-2 was required to be e-filed, which applies at 10 or more information returns in total. A wage correction may also require a Form 941-X.


For Forms W-2 due in 2027, the IRS penalty is $60 per form if the correct form is filed within 30 days of the due date, $130 if filed later but by August 1, and $340 after August 1 or if never filed, and at least $690 for intentional disregard, with a separate penalty for incorrect statements to employees (IRS information return penalties). These figures are as of October 2026.
What is a state unemployment tax notice of assessment?
A state unemployment tax notice of assessment is a state agency’s official notice of what an employer owes, and California, Texas and New York each use a different appeal process, with New York calling its notice a determination. California’s Employment Development Department (EDD) says its Notice of Assessment “serves as official notice of the EDD’s determination” in a misclassified-worker case (EDD DE 231MW). In Texas, the Texas Workforce Commission (TWC) guidebook lists “notice of assessment” among the compliance tools of the Texas Unemployment Compensation Act (TWC guidebook). New York uses a different word, and the Department of Labor’s hearing page refers to “a determination about your liability under the Unemployment Insurance Law.”
How long do I have to appeal a state unemployment tax assessment?
The appeal deadline varies by state and by notice, so an employer follows the agency’s own notice and confirms the timing with the agency. The examples below come from agency pages as of October 2026.


In California, a 2019 EDD information sheet on assessments for misclassified workers (DE 231MW, Rev. 8, 9-19) says a petition for reassessment to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB) “generally must be filed within 30 days after an assessment is issued” (EDD DE 231MW). The current Employers’ Bill of Rights (DE 195, Rev. 18, 9-26) says the notice explains the petition rights and to read all EDD notices because there are “different time frames to file appeals” (EDD DE 195). A petition does not suspend interest, and an employer may prepay the assessment, in which case the petition converts to a refund claim (EDD DE 1009).


In Texas, employers can request a Rule 13 hearing to dispute coverage, taxes or penalties by emailing a written request to the TWC Tax Department. TWC’s Rule 13 and guidebook pages state no number of days for making that request, so a Texas employer confirms the timing with the TWC Tax Department. TWC’s page says an employer may request a Motion for Reconsideration “within 30 calendar days after the date TWC mailed you the Commission decision” (TWC tax liability appeals).


In New York, an employer that disagrees with a liability determination submits the Employer Request for a Hearing with specific grounds “within 30 days after the mailing date” or personal delivery of the determination. For a hearing request based on audit or investigation results, the Department says interest continues to accrue on unpaid balances at 12 percent per year from the original due date to the date of payment (New York State Department of Labor).
How do I correct a state unemployment wage report?
California employers submit corrections through e-Services for Business, Texas employers adjust wage reports online or on paper forms, and New York employers file an amended Form NYS-45.


In California, the EDD says to submit adjustments through e-Services for Business even if the original was filed another way. The employer completes one Quarterly Contribution and Wage Adjustment Form (DE 9ADJ) per quarter, and the EDD says a refund claim is due by the latest of 3 years after the last timely date of the quarter being adjusted, 6 months after an assessment becomes final, and 60 days after the overpayment (EDD correction page).


In Texas, TWC’s online Unemployment Tax Services lets employers adjust previously filed wage reports for “quarters within the three-year statute of limitations,” out-of-statute corrections need a paper Form C-5 or C-7, and each adjustment needs “a valid and detailed reason” (TWC wage report adjustments).


In New York, an employer amends a Form NYS-45 by completing an amended form with the Amended return box marked. If the IRS changes an amount the employer must report as wages or withhold, the employer reports the change to the New York State Tax Department within 90 days after the final federal determination, on an amended NYS-45 with a copy of the final federal determination attached (Form NYS-45 instructions).
